## The problem

Support forwards you three messages in one morning. A user in Kochi says the feed "never loads, just spins." A user on hotel wifi says login fails instantly with "Network request failed." A third sends a screenshot of your generic error toast with no detail at all. You open the app on your desk: everything works. The API responds. You have no idea which of those three reports is even the same bug.

That confusion is not a networking gap, it is a *model* gap. Right now every failure between your app and a server collapses into one undifferentiated sentence: "the backend is broken." A request actually travels through six distinct stages, and each one fails in a way that looks different on the client. Once you can name the stages, a support message stops being noise and starts pointing at a layer.

## The idea

Calling `fetch()` is placing a phone call to a company's support line.

First you look up the number in your contacts — that is **DNS**, turning `api.example.com` into an IP address. Then the line rings and both sides say "hello, are you there?" before anyone talks — that is the **TCP handshake**. Then you both switch on a scrambler you each own so nobody on the line can listen in, and you check the other side's ID badge — that is **TLS**, which is the S in HTTPS. Only now do you speak, and you speak to a script they published: "account number first, then your request" — that is **HTTP**.

On the other end is not a building. It is a **process**: a program someone wrote, running on a machine that stays on, which asked the operating system for a port number and has been sitting in a loop waiting for calls. That is the whole mystery of "a server." You already write the client half every day. The server half is a program with the same kind of event loop, listening instead of calling.

## In practice

Here is the call you have written a hundred times.

```ts
const res = await fetch("https://api.example.com/v1/notes", {
  method: "GET",
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
});
const notes = await res.json();
```

Between the `await` and the response, this happens:

1. **DNS** — resolve `api.example.com` to something like `203.0.113.10`. Cached on the device, so usually free; occasionally stale for exactly one user.
2. **TCP** — open a connection to port 443 on that IP. Three packets, one round trip.
3. **TLS** — the server presents a certificate, both sides agree on keys. One or two more round trips. This is why the *first* request on a cold connection is slower than the next twenty.
4. **HTTP request** — method, path, headers, body, sent as bytes through the encrypted tunnel.
5. **Your server process** — accepts the connection, matches the path to a handler, runs code, probably queries a database.
6. **HTTP response** — status line, headers, body come back. The connection stays open (keep-alive) so the next call skips stages 1 to 3.

Now the payoff. Match the symptom to the stage:

| What you see on the client | Stage to suspect |
|---|---|
| Instant "Network request failed", other apps fine | DNS, or no route to that host at all |
| Hangs, then times out after 30s | Connection blocked, or the server accepted and never answered |
| 502 or 503 | The proxy was reached; your app process is down, crashing, or restarting |
| 504 | Proxy waited for your app and gave up; something is too slow |
| 401 or 403 | Your code ran; auth logic said no |
| 400 or 422 | Your code ran; the payload was wrong |
| 500 | Your code ran and threw |
| CORS error in a browser console | The response arrived; the browser refused to let JS read it |

Two of these are worth memorising. **500 versus 502**: a 500 means your code executed and raised an error, so there is a stack trace in your logs. A 502 means the proxy in front of your app could not get a valid response out of the process at all, so there is often *nothing* in your app logs — look at whether the process is alive. **CORS** is a browser rule, not a server failure. Native apps and `curl` ignore it entirely, and a CORS error almost always means the request did reach the server.

You can watch every stage from a terminal:

```bash
dig +short api.github.com

curl -v https://api.github.com/zen

curl -o /dev/null -s -w "dns:%{time_namelookup} tcp:%{time_connect} tls:%{time_appconnect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer} total:%{time_total}\n" https://api.github.com/zen
```

The third command is the one to keep. When someone says "the API is slow," those five numbers tell you whether it is the network or your code, before you open a single file.

## In your world

Your work backend runs as three processes behind a domain, so a request from the mobile app hits a proxy first and your API process second. That layout explains a class of incident you have probably witnessed without decoding: a deploy goes out with a bad environment variable, the process crashes on boot, and every user gets a 502. Your app's error handler has nothing useful to show because your code never ran — there is no error to report, only an absence. The fix is never in the app.

You will meet the smaller version of this tomorrow. When you start a server on port 3000 and open `localhost:3000` from the iOS simulator, it works, because the simulator shares your Mac's network. Do the same on a physical Android phone and it fails, because `localhost` on that phone means *that phone*. Nothing is wrong with your server. You dialled the wrong number. Recognising that as a stage-1 problem instead of a code problem is the entire skill this module is teaching.

## Watch out

- `localhost` is relative to whoever says it. Physical devices need your Mac's LAN IP; the Android emulator reaches the host at `10.0.2.2`.
- A timeout is not a message from the server. Nobody answered. Searching your application logs for it is usually wasted time — check first whether the process is running.
- HTTPS proves the tunnel is private and the server is who it claims. It proves nothing about the caller. Encryption is not authentication.
- Keep-alive means your timing measurements lie if you only run them once. The first request pays for DNS, TCP, and TLS; the rest do not.
tasks: Run the curl timing command from the lesson against https://api.github.com/zen twice in a row. Write down which phase dominated and why the second run is faster.
Run `curl -v https://api.github.com/zen` and label three things in the output: the TLS handshake lines, the request line you sent, and the response status line.

Produce two different failures on purpose: `curl -v https://not-a-real-host.invalid` and `curl -v http://localhost:9999`. Write down how the two error messages differ and which stage each one failed at.
Take one real network failure your app has had (Sentry, a support ticket, or memory) and place it on the symptom table. Say what you would check first and second.
Write the symptom-to-stage table from memory in your own notes, then compare against the lesson and fix what you got wrong.

quiz.q: Your app returns 'Network request failed' instantly, while a browser on the same phone loads other sites fine. Which stage do you suspect first?
options: DNS resolution, or no route to that host at all
Your route handler threw an exception
The database query is slow
A CORS misconfiguration on the server
quiz.explain: An instant failure means the request never got far enough to be answered. Nothing was sent and nothing timed out, which points at name resolution or reachability, not at your code.

quiz.q: A request hangs for 30 seconds and then times out on the client. What does that tell you?
options: The server returned a 504
Your error handler formatted the response badly
Nobody sent a response: the process may be dead, blocked, or unreachable
The client sent an invalid body
quiz.explain: A timeout is the absence of an answer, not a message from the server. There is no status code and often nothing in your application logs, so check first whether the process is alive and responsive.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a 500 and a 502?
options: They are interchangeable; different proxies pick different numbers
500 means your code ran and threw; 502 means the proxy could not get a valid response out of your process at all
502 always means DNS failed
500 is a client error and 502 is a server error
quiz.explain: A 500 leaves a stack trace in your logs because your handler executed. A 502 often leaves nothing, because the process was down, crashing, or restarting when the proxy tried to reach it.

quiz.q: A teammate reports that the mobile app is getting a CORS error. What is the right reaction?
options: Add the cors() middleware and the mobile bug is fixed
CORS is enforced by browsers, so a native app ignores it: the report is about a web client or a misread error message
CORS errors mean the request never left the device
A CORS error is a TLS handshake failure
quiz.explain: CORS is a browser rule about which origins may read a response. Native apps and curl ignore it entirely, and a genuine CORS error means the request did reach the server.

quiz.q: Your endpoint is served over HTTPS. What does that guarantee?
options: The caller is authenticated
The request body is valid
The bytes in transit are encrypted and the server's identity is verified; it says nothing about who is calling
You no longer need auth tokens for that endpoint
quiz.explain: TLS protects the tunnel and proves the server is who it claims to be. Identifying the caller is authentication, a completely separate job that happens inside your code.

## The problem

A user checks out on a train. He taps "Place order", the tunnel arrives, the spinner keeps spinning, and your app's 10-second timeout fires. Your networking layer does the sensible thing and retries. Two minutes later he has one order in his history and two charges on his card.

Nothing in that story is a bug in your retry code. The retry was correct. The bug is that `POST /orders` means "create another order," and you asked twice. The server never got a chance to know it was the same intent. The reverse mistake costs you differently: you spend an hour reading server code because your dashboard shows a spike of 500s, and the client was sending a malformed body all along. A 500 said "my fault" when it should have said "yours." Status codes are how two teams that never talk assign blame correctly.

## The idea

HTTP is a contract language with a deliberately small vocabulary. The **method** says what kind of operation this is. The **status code** says what happened and who owns the problem. **Headers** carry metadata about the message. The **body** carries the data.

You already trust a contract like this: the props of a shared component. If both sides agree on the shape, neither has to read the other's source. HTTP is that agreement standardised, so a proxy, a CDN, a monitoring tool, and your app can all reason about a request none of them wrote.

Two words carry most of the weight. A method is **safe** if it changes nothing on the server. A method is **idempotent** if doing it five times leaves the server in the same state as doing it once. Idempotent does not mean "returns the same response" — it means the *effect* does not accumulate.

## In practice

| Method | Safe | Idempotent | Means |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | yes | yes | read something |
| POST | no | no | create something, or trigger an action |
| PUT | no | yes | replace the thing at this known id |
| PATCH | no | no | partially update the thing at this id |
| DELETE | no | yes | remove the thing at this known id |

Read the DELETE row carefully, because it is where people get confused. `DELETE /notes/42` twice gives you a 204 and then a 404. Different status codes, same end state: note 42 is gone. That is exactly what idempotent means, and it is why a retry of a DELETE is harmless while a retry of a POST is not.

So how do you make a POST safe to retry? You give the *intent* an id, generated by the client at the moment the user acts.

```ts
// generated once, when the user taps the button — NOT inside the retry loop
const idempotencyKey = randomUUID();

await fetch(`${API}/orders`, {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({ cartId, totalCents }),
});
```

The server stores the key with the result it produced. On a replay it recognises the key and returns the stored response instead of charging again. Regenerating the key inside the retry makes every attempt look like a fresh intent, which is the same bug with extra ceremony. Stripe's API works exactly this way, and now you know why.

Status codes come in families, and the family is the important part:

| Family | Meaning | Who fixes it |
|---|---|---|
| 2xx | it worked | nobody |
| 3xx | look somewhere else | the client follows the pointer |
| 4xx | the request was wrong | the caller |
| 5xx | the server broke on a valid request | you |

The ones worth knowing cold when you are the one writing the API:

- **200** OK with a body. **201** Created, plus a `Location` header pointing at the new resource. **204** No Content, for a successful delete or an update with nothing to say.
- **400** malformed or failed validation. **422** well-formed but semantically impossible (a valid date that is in the past when it must be future).
- **401** versus **403**: 401 means "I do not know who you are" — no credentials, or expired ones. 403 means "I know exactly who you are and you may not do this." Your app's token-refresh interceptor should retry on 401 and must never retry on 403, because retrying a 403 is an infinite loop that logs the user out for no reason.
- **404** not found. **409** conflict — duplicate email, or a version clash on a concurrent edit. **429** too many requests, always with a `Retry-After` header so the client knows how long to wait.
- **500** you threw. **503** you are alive but not ready (starting up, dependency down).

Headers you will actually use: `Content-Type` (what the body is), `Authorization` (who is asking), `Accept` (what the caller can read), `Cache-Control` and `ETag` (how long this may be reused), `Retry-After`, and `Idempotency-Key`.

One rule to carry into every API you write: **never return 200 with an error inside the body.**

```ts
// bad: the transport says success, the payload says failure
res.status(200).json({ ok: false, message: "note not found" });

// good: the status is the answer, the body explains it
res.status(404).json({ error: "note_not_found", noteId: id });
```

The first version forces every caller to parse a body to learn whether the call worked, and it blinds your proxy, your retry logic, your dashboards, and your alerting. All of those read the status code. None of them read your JSON.

## In your world

Your practice projects give you both sides of this immediately. In task-manager-api, updating a task is where PUT and PATCH separate: PUT replaces the whole task (send every field, twice is fine), PATCH toggles `completed`. In marketplace-api, order creation is literally the double-charge story above, and it is where you will implement an idempotency key against a real payment flow rather than reading about one.

At work the contract is enforced by schema: routes declare their request shape and the status codes they can return, and that declaration generates the API description your mobile app consumes. So 4xx-versus-5xx discipline is not an academic preference — it *is* the quality of your own app's error messages. A route that throws an unmodelled error becomes a 500, your app shows the generic "something went wrong," and the user learns nothing. A route that returns a 409 with `{ error: "email_taken" }` lets your app say the one sentence that helps.

## Watch out

- Mixing up 401 and 403 makes your app log people out when they merely lacked permission.
- A retry after a network failure is not safe just because the request *looked* failed. The server may have processed it and the response may have been lost on the way back. That ambiguity is unavoidable, which is why the idempotency key exists.
- PATCH is not idempotent unless you design it to be. A body that says "increment views by 1" accumulates on every retry.
- Returning 404 instead of 403 to avoid leaking whether a resource exists is a legitimate choice. Make it deliberately and document it, do not stumble into it.
tasks: Write the five-method table with safe and idempotent columns from memory, then check it against the MDN methods reference and correct it.
Pick three endpoints your app calls today. For each, judge whether the method is right, whether the status codes are honest, and whether a retry is safe.
Find one place in your app where a POST can be sent twice (timeout retry, pull-to-refresh, a double-tappable button) and write the two-line plan for making it idempotent.
curl a real API for one 200, one 404, and one 401 (send a deliberately bad token). Record the body shape each one returns.
Write down the single error-response shape you will use for every project in this course: the field for the machine-readable code, the human message, and the field-level issues.

quiz.q: You send `DELETE /notes/42` twice. The first returns 204, the second returns 404. Is DELETE still idempotent?
options: No, because the status codes differ
Yes: idempotent is about the resulting state, not the response, and note 42 is gone either way
Only if the server returns 204 both times
Idempotency does not apply to DELETE
quiz.explain: Idempotent means repeating the request does not change the outcome further. The second call finds nothing to delete and says so, which is why retrying a DELETE is safe.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT idempotent?
options: PUT /notes/42 with the full replacement body
GET /notes/42
PATCH /notes/42 with a body meaning 'add 1 to the view count'
DELETE /notes/42
quiz.explain: A relative update accumulates: five retries add five views. PATCH is only idempotent if you design its body to describe an absolute end state.

quiz.q: Your app's interceptor refreshes the token and retries on failure. Which status must it never retry?
options: 401, because the token is expired
403, because the server already knows who you are and is refusing on purpose
429, because you are rate limited
500, because the server broke
quiz.explain: 403 means authenticated but not permitted, so refreshing the token changes nothing. Retrying it loops, and treating it like a 401 logs the user out for no reason.

quiz.q: Why should an API never return 200 with `{ ok: false }` in the body?
options: It uses more bandwidth
Proxies, retries, monitoring, and alerting all read the status code and would treat the failure as a success
JSON bodies are not allowed on error responses
It breaks TLS
quiz.explain: The status code is the part of the response that every layer between you and the client understands. Hiding failure in the body blinds all of them, and forces each caller to parse a body to learn whether the call worked.

quiz.q: Where should an idempotency key be generated?
options: On the server, once per received request
In the client, once per user intent, and reused by every retry of that intent
In the client, freshly inside each retry attempt
By the load balancer
quiz.explain: The key identifies the intent, not the transmission. Generating a new one per attempt makes every retry look like a new order, which is the exact bug it was supposed to prevent.

tasks: Scaffold hello-api with express, typescript and tsx, and get it listening on port 3000.
Write the raw node:http server first, curl it, then write down the three things Express adds on top of it.
Implement GET /health, GET /greet/:name with a loud query param, and POST /echo. curl all three with -i and record the status codes.
POST to /echo without the Content-Type header. Record what req.body is and explain why it is that and not an empty object.
Call your server from a real app or the iOS simulator using localhost, then from a physical device using your Mac's LAN IP. Note what breaks and why.
Cause EADDRINUSE deliberately by starting the server twice, then find and kill the first process with lsof instead of changing ports.
Declare /notes/:id before /notes/new, request /notes/new, and record which handler actually ran.

quiz.q: What is a 'server' in the most literal sense?
options: A machine in a data centre
A program that holds a port and waits in a loop for connections
A framework like Express
A container image
quiz.explain: It is a process, not a place. It asks the OS for a port and blocks until a connection arrives, which is why 'the server is down' usually means one program exited.

quiz.q: A client requests /notes?limit=20. What is the type of req.query.limit?
options: number, because Express parses numeric query values
string, always: URL values arrive as text and may also be undefined or an array
number | undefined
It depends on the Content-Type header
quiz.explain: Everything in a URL is text. Number(req.query.limit) gives NaN when the param is missing, which is why day 5 replaces hand-written casts with schema coercion.

quiz.q: Your server fails to start with EADDRINUSE. What happened?
options: The port number is above the allowed range
Another process, usually a previous run of your own server, already holds that port
Your firewall blocked the port
Express needs the port declared in package.json
quiz.explain: One process per port. Find the old one (lsof -i :3000) and kill it, rather than moving to a new port each time and losing track of what is running.

quiz.q: You declare app.get('/notes/:id') above app.get('/notes/new'). What happens on GET /notes/new?
options: Express prefers the more specific literal route
The :id handler runs with id set to the string 'new'
Express returns a 404
Both handlers run in order
quiz.explain: Routes match top to bottom, first match wins, and :id matches any single segment. Literal paths must be declared before the parameterised route that would swallow them.

quiz.q: Your API works from the iOS simulator at localhost:3000 but not from a physical Android phone on the same wifi. Why?
options: Android does not support fetch
localhost on the phone means the phone; the phone needs your Mac's LAN IP (and the emulator reaches the host at 10.0.2.2)
Express only binds to IPv6
The server needs HTTPS before any device can call it
quiz.explain: localhost is relative to whoever says it. This is a stage-1 addressing problem, not a bug in your server, and recognising the difference is the point of day 1.

tasks: Write requestLog, requireAuth, notFound and errorHandler as separate files, then assemble app.ts in the exact order from the lesson.
Type req.user by augmenting Express's Request interface. Do it without using any.
Run today's trap in full, including the async rejection, and write the three-line symptom lookup table it asks for.
Mount requireAuth on a router so every route inside it is protected by construction, then prove with curl that /health is public and the protected route returns 401.
Delete the `return` in front of one res.status(401) call, hit that route, and record the second error Express reports. Put the return back.
Send a request with a valid token and confirm your log line contains the method, path, status and duration for exactly one request.

quiz.q: A middleware inspects the request, decides everything is fine, and returns without calling next() or sending a response. What does the client see?
options: A 500 with a stack trace
Nothing: the request hangs until the client times out, and no error is logged anywhere
A 404 from the not-found handler
Express calls next() automatically after the function returns
quiz.explain: Nothing went wrong, so nothing is reported. The request simply stops moving. This is the failure mode with the worst signal-to-effort ratio in Express, which is why you trigger it deliberately today.

quiz.q: Where must the error handler be registered?
options: First, so it can catch everything below it
Last, after all routes: middleware runs in registration order and errors travel forward, not backward
Anywhere, Express finds it by name
Twice, once at the top and once at the bottom
quiz.explain: The pipeline is ordered top to bottom. An error handler above the routes is never reached, and you get Express's default HTML error page instead of your JSON shape.

quiz.q: How does Express know a function is an error handler rather than normal middleware?
options: It checks the function name
By its arity: four parameters (err, req, res, next)
You register it with app.error()
It must be exported as default
quiz.explain: Four declared parameters is the signal, which is why you keep the unused ones in the signature instead of trimming them.

quiz.q: Your native app gets a network error and someone suggests adding cors(). What is true?
options: CORS headers are needed by every HTTP client
CORS is enforced by browsers only, so adding it cannot fix a native-client problem
cors() also enables preflight for mobile apps
CORS must be registered after the routes
quiz.explain: CORS headers tell a browser which origins may read a response. Native clients and curl ignore them, so a CORS change is invisible to your app.

quiz.q: What is the difference between next() and next(err)?
options: Nothing; the argument is ignored
next() continues to the next station in the line; next(err) skips the remaining stations and jumps to the error handler
next(err) retries the request
next(err) sends a 500 immediately and ends the response
quiz.explain: Passing a value is a control-flow decision: everything between here and the error handler is skipped. That is how you forward a caught async error deliberately.

tasks: Write env.ts with a Zod schema, then boot the app with DATABASE_URL removed and confirm the process refuses to start and exits non-zero.
Write logger.ts with pino: level from LOG_LEVEL, pretty transport in development only, redaction for the authorization header and any password or token field.
Write the validateBody middleware with safeParse and wire it to a POST route whose schema requires a non-empty title.
Send three bad bodies (missing field, wrong type, empty string) and record the exact 400 payload each one produces.
Add a query schema using z.coerce.number for limit, then request limit=abc and limit=9999 and record both responses.
Add the request-id middleware and prove that two log lines from the same request share one id, and that the id comes back in a response header.
Replace every console.log in the project with a logger call, then set LOG_LEVEL=warn and confirm the info lines disappear without a code change.

quiz.q: A route calls schema.parse(req.body) and the body is invalid. What does the client get, with no other changes?
options: A 400 with the validation issues
A 500, because parse throws and an unhandled ZodError is just another exception
A 422 automatically
An empty 200
quiz.explain: parse throws. Unless your error handler knows about ZodError, the caller's mistake is reported as your server breaking. safeParse at the boundary returns a result you turn into an honest 400.

quiz.q: Why validate environment variables at startup instead of at the point of use?
options: It is faster at runtime
A misconfigured process then fails immediately and loudly, so a pipeline rolls it back, instead of failing on some request hours later
Because process.env is read-only
So you can commit the values to git safely
quiz.explain: Crash-on-boot is a feature. The alternative is a green deploy that starts 500ing on the first request that happens to touch the missing config, usually after you have logged off.

quiz.q: What is the strongest technical argument against console.log in a server?
options: It is slower to type than logger.info
It has no levels, emits unsearchable prose, and writes synchronously to a pipe or file, which blocks the event loop under load
It cannot print objects
It is removed in production builds
quiz.explain: All three matter, and the blocking write is the one that surprises people: in a container, stdout is a pipe, and heavy logging becomes your throughput ceiling.

quiz.q: What does z.infer give you that writing the interface by hand does not?
options: Faster parsing
One declaration that is both the runtime check and the compile-time type, so the two cannot drift apart
Automatic 400 responses
Database migrations
quiz.explain: Two parallel definitions always diverge eventually, and the divergence is invisible until production. Deriving the type from the schema makes that impossible.

quiz.q: Why use z.coerce.number() for a query param instead of z.number()?
options: z.number() is deprecated
Query values always arrive as strings, so a plain number schema would reject every request
coerce also validates the range
It makes the field optional
quiz.explain: The URL carries text. Coercion converts at the boundary so everything downstream sees a real number, which is the proper fix for hand-written Number() casts.

tasks: Build notes.store.ts, notes.schema.ts, notes.service.ts and notes.routes.ts, each with only the responsibility described in the lesson.
Implement POST /notes (201 plus Location), GET /notes, GET /notes/:id and DELETE /notes/:id (204), with Zod validation on the create body.
Make DELETE set deletedAt, then confirm GET /notes excludes the note and GET /notes/:id returns 404 rather than a note with a deletedAt field.
Grep notes.routes.ts for deletedAt and confirm zero hits. If there are any, move the rule down into the service.
Run the hard-delete trap end to end, then remove the hard-delete code from the project.
Swap the store's array for a Map without editing notes.service.ts or notes.routes.ts. If you had to edit them, fix the boundary that leaked.
Answer all six checkpoint questions out loud with the editor closed. Record yourself and note every answer that came out vague.

quiz.q: Which of these belongs in the service, not the route?
options: Choosing between 404 and 200
Deciding that a note with a deletedAt timestamp counts as not found
Reading the id out of req.params
Setting the Location response header
quiz.explain: That is a rule about what a note is, so it belongs where the rules live. The route's job is only to translate the service's outcome into HTTP.

quiz.q: Why does the service return `{ ok: false, reason: 'not_found' }` instead of throwing a NotFoundError?
options: Throwing is slower
A missing row is an ordinary, expected outcome of a lookup; exceptions are for things you did not plan for, and a returned union forces every caller to handle the case
Express cannot catch exceptions
So the route can ignore the failure case
quiz.explain: The discriminated union makes the failure part of the type, so a caller that forgets to handle it does not compile. A thrown error is invisible to the type system.

quiz.q: What does soft delete buy you that a hard delete cannot?
options: Faster reads
An audit trail, a one-line undo, and rows elsewhere that reference the id still resolving to real content
Smaller database size
Automatic cascading to child rows
quiz.explain: The row keeps existing, so you can still answer who deleted it, when, and what it said, and comments or attachments pointing at it do not become dangling references.

quiz.q: Why is the notes array not exported from the store module?
options: Exports are slow
Because if any other file can reach the array, the store's functions stop being the only way in and swapping in a database stops being a one-file change
TypeScript forbids exporting arrays
So the array can be mutated safely
quiz.explain: Encapsulation is what makes the data layer replaceable. Every direct reader of the raw array is another file you must edit on migration day.

quiz.q: Which layer is allowed to know about status codes?
options: All three, so each can fail properly
Only the route: the service returns outcomes, and the store returns data or undefined
Only the service, since it knows what went wrong
Only the error handler
quiz.explain: HTTP stops at the route. A service that returns 404 cannot be called from a worker or a CLI script without dragging HTTP semantics into places that have no requests.

quiz.q: Why type a catch parameter as unknown rather than any?
options: unknown is faster at runtime
any lets you access properties that may not exist, so you can throw a TypeError inside your own error handler
unknown automatically converts errors to strings
any is not allowed in catch clauses
quiz.explain: With any, err.response.data.message compiles and then explodes at the worst moment. unknown forces you to prove what you caught before you read it.

quiz.q: What does `as const` change about `const ROLES = ['user', 'admin']`?
options: It freezes the array at runtime only
The type becomes a readonly tuple of literals, so you can derive a 'user' | 'admin' union from it instead of getting string[]
It makes the array mutable
Nothing, it is a style preference
quiz.explain: Without it the element type is string and any derived type collapses to string. With it, one list serves as both the runtime check and the type.

quiz.q: What does a discriminated union result type give you that a thrown error does not?
options: Better stack traces
The compiler enforces that every caller handles every failure case, and adding a new case breaks the build instead of failing silently
Automatic HTTP status mapping
Faster execution
quiz.explain: Failure becomes part of the signature. On a server, where there is no screen to show you the mistake, the compiler is the feedback loop you have.
